title: Contract verbs

objectives.can: Recognise the present forms of verbs in -έω, -άω and -όω and name their uncontracted headword.

explanation.summary: Verbs whose stem ends in -ε, -α or -ο, such as ποιέω, ἀγαπάω and δηλόω, run that vowel together with the vowel of the ending. The result is a set of endings that look different from λέγω's, but follow a small number of rules.

sections.heading: What 'contract' means
body: In a verb like λύω the stem meets the ending without trouble. In a contract verb the stem ends in a vowel, and in the present and imperfect that vowel meets the vowel of the ending. Greek avoids the clash by contracting the two into one vowel or diphthong. The contraction is regular, so the same few rules explain every form.

Lexica and vocabulary lists give the uncontracted headword: ποιέω, ἀγαπάω, πληρόω. You will almost never see those spellings in a text. What you will see is the contracted form: ποιῶ, ἀγαπῶ, ποιοῦμεν. Working backwards from the contracted form to the headword is the main skill of this lesson.

sections.heading: The contractions
body: Take the stem vowel (ε, α or ο), add the vowel of the ending, and read off the result from the table. The table lists only the endings that occur in the present indicative. Where the first vowel is accented the new syllable usually has a circumflex, which is why contract verbs are full of circumflexes.

sections.heading: The present endings after contraction
body: Put the stem vowel and each personal ending of the previous lesson through the table, and you have the full set. Most forms show the type at once: -εῖ and -εῖς point to an -έω verb (ποιεῖ); -ᾷ and -ᾷς point to an -άω verb (ἀγαπᾷ); -οῖ and -οῖς point to an -όω verb (δηλοῖ).

The first person singular does not tell you the type. A form ending in -ῶ may come from any of the three, and you need the stem or a lexicon to decide: ποιῶ is from ποιέω, ἀγαπῶ from ἀγαπάω. The same is true of the third person plural of -έω and -όω verbs, which both end in -οῦσι(ν).

sections.heading: Which verbs are which
body: Verbs in -έω are by far the commonest in the New Testament (ποιέω, λαλέω, καλέω, ζητέω, ἀκολουθέω, μαρτυρέω). Verbs in -άω (ἀγαπάω, γεννάω, ἐρωτάω, ὁράω) are fewer. Verbs in -όω (πληρόω, σταυρόω, φανερόω) are mostly verbs that mean 'make something so' and are very often met in the aorist and the passive. Their present active is rare in the texts, so the paradigms below show only -έω and -άω; for -όω, learn the endings from the second table and look for them in the reading.

Two verbs are irregular. ζάω contracts to η instead of α, so it has ζῶ, ζῇς, ζῇ, ζῶμεν, ζῆτε, ζῶσιν. And ὁράω is a regular -άω verb in the present (ὁρῶ, ὁρᾷ), but its other tenses are formed from quite different stems, which you will meet later.

sections.heading: Reading contract forms
body: The subject is still in the ending. Read the person and number as you did in the previous lesson: -εῖς, -ᾷς, -οῖς are second person singular; -οῦμεν and -ῶμεν are first person plural; -οῦσιν and -ῶσιν are third person plural. The only new work is finding the headword.

misunderstandings: Contraction does not change the meaning or the kind of form. ποιεῖς is simply 'you (singular) do', in the same tense-form as λέγεις. Only the spelling changes.
The uncontracted headword is not a form that was ever read in the text. ποιέω is the label under which the dictionary files all the forms. Do not look for it in a verse.

A contracted form can have the same spelling as a form from another mood. ποιεῖτε is both a present indicative ('you do') and a present imperative ('do!'), and ἀγαπᾶτε can be indicative, imperative or subjunctive. Spelling alone does not decide; the context does. This lesson asks only about the indicative.
Do not force ζάω into the -άω pattern. Where ἀγαπάω gives ἀγαπᾷ and ἀγαπᾶτε, ζάω gives ζῇ and ζῆτε, so the third person singular ζῇ is not a form of any other verb.

deeper.heading: Why the vowels contract
body: In the oldest Greek the stem vowel and the vowel of the ending were pronounced separately, and Homer still has uncontracted forms. In Attic Greek the two vowels contracted, and the contracted spellings are the ones the New Testament and later writers use. A reader needs only the table above.

examples.analysis: ποιοῦμεν is first person plural, present active indicative, from ποιέω. The stem vowel ε and the ending vowel ο contract to ου: the stem ποιε- with the ending -ομεν gives ποιοῦμεν. 'We do not do the truth' is the claim that the verse tests.

examples.analysis: ἀγαπῶμεν is first person plural, present active indicative, from ἀγαπάω (α and ο contract to ω). ἀγαπῶν later in the verse is a participle of the same verb ('loving'), not a finite form: it has no person. μένει is an ordinary, uncontracted verb, third person singular, from μένω.

options: Only that it is a contract verb: -ῶ could come from -έω, -άω or -όω
check.explain: All three types give -ῶ in the first person singular. Here the verb is φιλέω, but you can only know that from the stem or the lexicon.

reading.why: Three verses built round contract verbs: ἀγαπάω and φιλέω in the second and first person, with λέγει, οἶδας and γινώσκεις in the same speeches for comparison. Whether the two verbs of loving differ in sense here is a question scholars debate; this lesson asks only that you can parse them.
